teaser.text: Prudential Financial is a financial company that takes in money today to protect, invest, or pay people later. Its businesses look varied, but the central question is always the same: who pays Prudential, what promise does Prudential accept, and what makes the dollar leave again?

blocks.heading: Where could Prudential's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: Bear probability is 30%. Base probability is 55%. Bull probability is 15%. Japan’s recovery, customer flows, expenses, capital generation, PGIM growth and efficiency savings decide the outcome. Prudential reports third-quarter 2026 earnings on November 3 and holds its call on November 4. Improvement plans are due by the end of November 2026; restrictions run through January 31, 2027. Reopening is expected over roughly 12–18 months, with 2027 sales at about 25% of 2025 levels.

The forecast points to modest weighted gains, but the outcomes spread widely. The weighted price is $114.57 in October 2027 and $122.98 in October 2028. It reaches $137.55 in October 2029. With dividends, those prices represent returns of 4% and 16%. The three-year return is 34%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Prudential?

paragraphs.text: The bear case assumes that Japan’s restrictions and trust repair weigh on earnings beyond reopening, while PGIM outflows and weaker investment results reduce capital and confidence. It gives $83.35 in October 2027 and $75.34 in October 2029. Its overall probability is 30% because the downside is severe, but Japan’s restrictions, estimated business impacts and market-sensitive equity make it credible.

The bull case requires faster Japan remediation, PGIM asset gathering and efficiency savings. It rises from $142.80 in 2027 to $204.78 in 2029. Its 15% probability is lower because several uncertain improvements must occur together, including buybacks above the stated 2026 authorization.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Prudential really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash flow reached $6,271 million in 2025, but it is not automatically available to shareholders. Policyholder flows, investment purchases, claims, commissions and statutory capital needs absorb cash. Parent liquidity is the sharper test of debt-service capacity: highly liquid parent assets fell by $824 million to $3,817 million at year-end 2025. Meanwhile, fewer diluted shares helped per-share growth exceed aggregate earnings growth.

blocks.heading: How much does Prudential pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Investment income and operating ROE strengthened through 2025; operating ROE reached 14.9%. Net premiums earned fell 28.2% in 2025, confirming that revenue is lumpy. The turn begins with the 2022 diluted loss and reaches 2025 EPS of $9.99. Dividends and buybacks left $1.70 per share retained in 2025.

blocks.heading: Is Prudential's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Those accounting flows are not the same as cash available at headquarters. Premiums and annuity deposits support customers’ future benefits, so regulated insurance subsidiaries must hold capital against market losses, deaths, withdrawals and guarantees. Only money safely above those requirements can generally move to the parent as a dividend.

paragraphs.text: The base dividend rises to $5.60 in 2027 and $5.80 in 2028. It reaches $6.00 in 2029, continuing the recent $0.20 annual increases. The bear freezes it at $5.40 because Japan and investment pressures could limit remittances. The bull reaches $5.80 and $6.20, then $6.60, assuming faster recovery. The freeze remains plausible because the 2025 payout was already 82.9% of common earnings, although management targets attractive and increasing dividends.

The bull case would gain support if efficiency benefits approach the targeted $750 million pretax run-rate by year-end 2028 and PGIM reaches 25% of adjusted operating income. Sustained earnings, parent liquidity above the $3,000 million minimum and continued buybacks would then justify higher book value and a stronger multiple.

blocks.heading: What is Prudential's dividend yield against its share price?

paragraphs.text: The 7.6x core-earnings multiple implies an earnings yield of about 13.2%. That is profit represented by each invested dollar, not a promised cash return. The 4.8% dividend yield is only one part of the earning power; the rest must support capital, growth, debt and other needs.

blocks.heading: What has Prudential guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management targets adjusted operating ROE of 13%–15% for 2025–2027. It wants PGIM at 25% of adjusted operating income over multiple years and margins above 30% over time. It also targets a $750 million pretax efficiency-benefit run-rate by year-end 2028. Parent highly liquid assets have a $3,000 million ongoing minimum. Japan’s estimated impact is $500 million in 2026. It is $500 million–$550 million in 2027.

Japan is the immediate counterweight. Prudential of Japan’s impact is about $500 million pretax in 2026 and $500 million–$550 million in 2027. Gibraltar adds $100 million in 2026 and $175 million in 2027. These figures combine lost earnings and expenses, so the test is whether growth elsewhere can offset them.

blocks.heading: How have Prudential's results changed over the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: Net income rose from $533 million in second-quarter 2025 to $985 million in second-quarter 2026. Core earnings rose more moderately, from $1,284 million to $1,438 million.

The annual assumption review charged GAAP income $299 million after tax while benefiting operating income by $51 million. Excluding the reviews, core earnings rose from $1,320 million to $1,387 million. PGIM improved and Group Insurance benefited from mortality, but expense, underwriting and Japan-related pressures remained uneven. The latest quarter therefore points to progress, not a clean acceleration.

blocks.heading: What should you watch in Prudential's next results?

paragraphs.text: Prudential will release third-quarter earnings on November 3, 2026, followed by its call on November 4. Investors will need customer flows, expenses and capital alongside the preliminary investment-income figures. Restated comparisons also matter because Brazil and Mexico are moving into divested and run-off businesses, while the former International segment becomes Japan Businesses.
